newsitem.title: UK: SALVORS AGREE TALKS ON NEW MARINE SALVAGE CONTRACT.
newsitem.headline: SALVORS AGREE TALKS ON NEW MARINE SALVAGE CONTRACT.

text.p: Members of the International Salvage Union (ISU) have agreed to open talks with P&I clubs, shipowners and insurers to develop a new salvage contract.
The marine salvors' association said the move was intended to preserve the best elements of the existing contract and incorporate elements of a new contract drawn up by P&I clubs.
The ISU's annual general meeting in Gothenburg this week agreed that its negotiators should offer an agreed rate structure for salvage services in cases presenting a pollution threat.
Salvors also agree to back P&I clubs' desire for separate representation at salvage arbitration cases arising from such incidents.
The existing Lloyd's Open Form (LOF) is the world's most commonly used salvage contract, the ISU said.
However, P&I clubs have drawn up a new contract, Salvage 2000, to safeguard levels of P&I involvement in casualty salvage.

ISU president Arnold Witte said: "In the ISU's view, the provisions of a new LOF/Salvage 2000 contract should be drafted to maximise opportunities for amicable settlement and prompt payment, without recourse to arbitration."

He added: "I am confident we can find a way to move forward on a basis that recognises the common interest of all sides - a new commercial framework promoting operational success and the prevention of marine spills."
The ISU said the LOF system still offered many advantages to the international shipping community and its underwriters.

However, it acknowledged that P&I clubs, who have financial responsibility for pollution claims arising from shipping accidents, have a number of legitimate concerns which cannot be ignored by the salvage industry.
"These concerns relate to cost and the level of P&I involvement in casualty salvage," Mr Witte said.

"As starting points, the ISU is to offer an agreed rates structure for salvage services deployed to deal with direct pollution threats and, secondly to support the P&I clubs' desire for separate representation at salvage arbitrations arising from such cases."

Mr Witte said: "After much consideration, the ISU has concluded that it is possible to develop provisions that preserve the best features of the existing system yet also include elements of the Salvage 2000 concept which would address the concern of the P&I Clubs."
The ISU represents 47 salvage companies in 33 countries world-wide.
